items.title: A projection in 3D
items.question: Find $\mathbf{p}$, $\mathbf{e}$ and the distance from $\mathbf{b}$ to the line.

explain.text: $x = 18 / 9 = 2$, so $\mathbf{p} = (4, -2, 4)$ and $\mathbf{e} = (-1, 2, 2)$, with $\mathbf{e} \cdot \mathbf{a} = -2 - 2 + 4 = 0$. The distance is $|\mathbf{e}| = 3$.

items.title: A family of lines
items.prose: The line runs along $\mathbf{a} = (1, k)$ for a number $k$.
items.question: Write the top-right entry of the projection matrix $\mathbf{P}$ in terms of $k$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the entry of $\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^T$, then divide by $\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{a}$.

byKey.nodiv: $k$ is the entry of $\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^T$. Divide by $\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{a} = 1 + k^2$.
byKey.len: You divided by $|\mathbf{a}|$. Divide by $|\mathbf{a}|^2 = 1 + k^2$.

explain.text: $\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^T = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & k \\ k & k^2 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{a} = 1 + k^2$, so the entry is $\dfrac{k}{1 + k^2}$. At $k = 1$ it is $\tfrac{1}{2}$, and as $k \to \infty$ it tends to 0: the line turns towards the $y$-axis.

items.title: Onto a plane
items.prose: $\mathbf{A}$ has columns $(1, 0, 1)$ and $(0, 1, 1)$, and $\mathbf{b} = (0, 0, 3)$. Use $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$, whose inverse is $\tfrac{1}{3}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$.
items.question: Find $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ and the projection $\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{A}\hat{\mathbf{x}}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{b} = (3, 3)$; multiply by the inverse, then by $\mathbf{A}$.

items.title: Why P squared is P
items.question: Put the lines of the proof in order.

lines.text: $= \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A})^{-1}\mathbf{A}^T = \mathbf{P}$, since a matrix times its inverse is $\mathbf{I}$
$\mathbf{P}^T = (\mathbf{A}^T)^T\,[(\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A})^{-1}]^T\mathbf{A}^T$, reversing the order of a transposed product
$= \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A})^{-1}\mathbf{A}^T = \mathbf{P}$, as $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$ is symmetric, so its inverse is too

feedback.correct: Both properties follow from the formula alone.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Finish $\mathbf{P}^2$ first: write it out, group the middle, cancel. Then transpose.

explain.text: The middle $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$ meets its own inverse and cancels, which is why projecting twice changes nothing. For the transpose, $(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{Z})^T = \mathbf{Z}^T\mathbf{Y}^T\mathbf{X}^T$, and the symmetric middle factor is its own transpose.

items.title: Hedging a stock
items.prose: Four days of returns, in %: market $\mathbf{m} = (2, -1, 0, 1)$ and a stock $\mathbf{s} = (2.5, -1.5, 0.5, 1)$. Ignore average returns. You hedge by shorting $\beta$ units of the market.
items.question: Find $\beta$ and the hedged returns $\mathbf{s} - \beta\mathbf{m}$ on days 2 and 3.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. $\beta = \mathbf{m} \cdot \mathbf{s} / \mathbf{m} \cdot \mathbf{m}$; then subtract $\beta\mathbf{m}$ day by day.

explain.text: $\beta = 1.25$, and the hedged returns $(0, -0.25, 0.5, -0.25)$ have dot product $0 + 0.25 + 0 - 0.25 = 0$ with $\mathbf{m}$. The hedge strips out every move along the market and leaves the idiosyncratic part.

items.title: Least squares from scratch with QR
items.prose: $\mathbf{A}$ has columns $\mathbf{a}_1 = (2, 2, 1)$ and $\mathbf{a}_2 = (3, 6, 0)$, and $\mathbf{b} = (0, 9, 0)$. Run Gram-Schmidt, build $\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{A}$, then solve $\mathbf{R}\hat{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{b}$.
items.question: Fill in $\mathbf{R}$, $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{b}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$.

explain.text: $\mathbf{q}_1 = \tfrac{1}{3}(2, 2, 1)$ and $\mathbf{q}_2 = \tfrac{1}{3}(-1, 2, -2)$, so $\mathbf{R} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 6 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{b} = (6, 6)$. Back substitution gives $\hat{x}_2 = 2$ and $\hat{x}_1 = -2$. Then $\mathbf{p} = (2, 8, -2)$ and $\mathbf{e} = (-2, 1, 2)$, perpendicular to both columns.

items.title: How bad is AᵀA
items.prose: Columns $(1, 1, 1)$ and $(1, 1.001, 0.999)$ give a design matrix with condition number about 2,449.
items.question: About what is the condition number of $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Forming $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$ squares the condition number.

byKey.same: That is $\kappa(\mathbf{A})$, which QR keeps. $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$ squares it.
byKey.double: The condition number is squared, not doubled.
byKey.root: That is the square root. Forming the product makes it worse, not better.

explain.text: $\kappa(\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}) = \kappa(\mathbf{A})^2 \approx 6 \times 10^6$. Double precision carries about 16 digits, so the normal equations lose about 7 of them, QR about 3.4.

options.why: The inverse in the middle does not disappear. Split it: $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^{-1}(\mathbf{A}^T)^{-1}\mathbf{A}^T$.
Projecting onto all of $\mathbb{R}^3$ removes nothing, so nothing is sent to $\mathbf{0}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. When $\mathbf{A}$ is square and invertible, $(\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A})^{-1} = \mathbf{A}^{-1}(\mathbf{A}^T)^{-1}$.

explain.text: An invertible 3 × 3 matrix has $C(\mathbf{A}) = \mathbb{R}^3$, so every $\mathbf{b}$ is its own projection and $\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{I}$. The same cancelling fails for a tall $\mathbf{A}$, which has no inverse.

items.title: A regression, explained by projection
items.prompt:
Four days of returns, in %: market $\mathbf{m} = (-1, 0, 1, 2)$ and a fund $\mathbf{y} = (-1, 1, 1, 3)$. You fit $y \approx \alpha + \beta m$ by least squares.

(a) Write the design matrix, form the normal equations $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}\hat{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{y}$ and solve them for $\alpha$ and $\beta$.

(b) Find the residual vector $\mathbf{e}$. Check $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{0}$ and say what each of its two entries means for the residuals.

(c) Prove that no other line $a + bm$ has a smaller sum of squared residuals, and illustrate with $a = 0$, $b = 1.5$.

(d) Explain why a statistics library would solve this with a QR factorisation rather than the normal equations.
items.model:
**(a) The fit.** The design matrix has columns $\mathbf{1} = (1, 1, 1, 1)$ and $\mathbf{m} = (-1, 0, 1, 2)$, and $\mathbf{y} = (-1, 1, 1, 3)$.

$$\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 6 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{y} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 8 \end{pmatrix}$$

since $\mathbf{1} \cdot \mathbf{1} = 4$, $\mathbf{1} \cdot \mathbf{m} = 2$, $\mathbf{m} \cdot \mathbf{m} = 6$, $\mathbf{1} \cdot \mathbf{y} = 4$ and $\mathbf{m} \cdot \mathbf{y} = 1 + 0 + 1 + 6 = 8$.

The normal equations are $4\alpha + 2\beta = 4$ and $2\alpha + 6\beta = 8$. Doubling the second and subtracting the first gives $10\beta = 12$, so $\beta = 1.2$. Then $4\alpha = 4 - 2.4$, so $\alpha = 0.4$.

**(b) Residuals.** Fitted values $0.4 + 1.2m$ are $(-0.8, 0.4, 1.6, 2.8)$, so

$$\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}} = (-0.2, 0.6, -0.6, 0.2).$$

Check: $\mathbf{1} \cdot \mathbf{e} = -0.2 + 0.6 - 0.6 + 0.2 = 0$ and $\mathbf{m} \cdot \mathbf{e} = 0.2 + 0 - 0.6 + 0.4 = 0$. So $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{0}$. The residuals sum to zero (the intercept column) and are uncorrelated with the market (the market column). The sum of squared residuals is $0.04 + 0.36 + 0.36 + 0.04 = 0.8$.

**(c) Why no other line does better.** Any other line $a + bm$ gives fitted values $\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{A}(a, b)$ in $C(\mathbf{A})$. Write $\mathbf{p} = \hat{\mathbf{y}}$. Then

$$\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{q} = \mathbf{e} + (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{q}),$$

and $\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{q} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{z}$ for $\mathbf{z} = (\alpha - a, \beta - b)$. The cross term is $\mathbf{e} \cdot \mathbf{A}\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{z}^T\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{e} = 0$. Expanding the square,

$$|\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{q}|^2 = |\mathbf{e}|^2 + |\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{q}|^2 \ge |\mathbf{e}|^2 = 0.8,$$

with equality only when $\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{p}$. For example, $a = 0$ and $b = 1.5$ give $\mathbf{q} = (-1.5, 0, 1.5, 3)$. Its squared error is $0.25 + 1 + 0.25 + 0 = 1.5$. That is $0.8 + 0.7$, since $|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{q}|^2 = 0.49 + 0.16 + 0.01 + 0.04 = 0.7$.

**(d) How software should solve it.** Forming $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$ squares the condition number of $\mathbf{A}$. Regressors can be nearly collinear: two highly correlated factors, or a market return and a sector return. Then the small differences between columns can be lost to rounding in $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$. QR factors $\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{R}$ and solves the triangular system $\mathbf{R}\hat{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{y}$ by back substitution. $\mathbf{R}$ has the same condition number as $\mathbf{A}$. It gives the same answer in exact arithmetic and loses about half as many digits in floating point.

rubric.text: Writes $\mathbf{A}$ with columns $\mathbf{1}$ and $\mathbf{m}$, and computes $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 6 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{y} = (4, 8)$
Checks $\mathbf{1} \cdot \mathbf{e} = 0$ and $\mathbf{m} \cdot \mathbf{e} = 0$, and interprets them: residuals sum to zero, and are uncorrelated with the market
Splits $\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{q} = \mathbf{e} + (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{q})$ and shows the cross term is 0 using $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{0}$, with a justification for each step
Concludes $|\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{q}|^2 \ge |\mathbf{e}|^2$ with equality only at $\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{p}$, and checks $1.5 = 0.8 + 0.7$ for $a = 0$, $b = 1.5$

Explains that forming $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$ squares the condition number, while QR solves $\mathbf{R}\hat{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{y}$ with $\mathbf{R}$ as well conditioned as $\mathbf{A}$

items.title: Strip the factors out of a signal
items.question: Write `project_out(F, s)` so it returns `(P, fitted, neutral)`.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np

def project_out(F, s):
    """Return (P, fitted, neutral) for factor matrix F and signal s."""
    F = np.array(F, dtype=float)
    s = np.array(s, dtype=float)
    k = F.shape[1]
    if np.linalg.matrix_rank(F) < k:
        raise ValueError("the factor columns are dependent")
    Q, R = np.linalg.qr(F)        # reduced: Q is n x k, orthonormal columns
    P = Q @ Q.T                   # n x n projection onto C(F)
    fitted = P @ s
    neutral = s - fitted
    return P, fitted, neutral

tests.call: [np.asarray(v, dtype=float).tolist() for v in project_out(F, s)[0::2]]

widget.how: Check runs 13 hidden tests on eight small factor sets. Arrays are compared entry by entry with math.isclose, within 1e-9. The tests read what your function returns, not how it finds it. The first run loads NumPy, which takes a few seconds.

feedback.correct: Right on every factor set, including the three that must be refused.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. On the example, the neutral signal is each score minus its own sector's mean.

byKey.test-1: The neutral signal is off. With a ones column and one sector flag, it is each score minus its own sector's mean: $(1, -1, 2, -2)$, not `fitted` minus `s`.
byKey.test-2: `fitted` is off. Here it is each stock's sector mean, $(2, 2, 3, 3)$. Adding the projections onto each column separately works only when the columns are perpendicular.
byKey.test-3: `P` is off. It should be $\tfrac12$ in each 2 by 2 sector block and 0 elsewhere. Check that it is $n \times n$ and that the inverse of $\mathbf{F}^T\mathbf{F}$ sits in the middle.
byKey.test-4: The neutral signal is off for three factors. Every factor counts at once, through $(\mathbf{F}^T\mathbf{F})^{-1}$ or the $\mathbf{Q}$ of a QR factorisation.
byKey.test-5: `fitted` is off for three factors. It should be $(4, 3, 3.5, 1.5, 0.5, 2.5)$.
byKey.test-6: $\mathbf{F}^T$ times your neutral signal is not $\mathbf{0}$, so some factor exposure is left in it.
byKey.test-7: `P` should be 6 by 6, with $\mathbf{P}^2 = \mathbf{P}$ and $\mathbf{P}^T = \mathbf{P}$. With $\mathbf{Q}$ from QR, that is `Q @ Q.T`, not `Q.T @ Q`.
byKey.test-8: Three independent factors on three stocks span every direction, so `P` is $\mathbf{I}$ and the neutral signal is $\mathbf{0}$. A transpose may be missing.
byKey.test-9: A ones column beside one flag per sector is dependent: the two flags add up to the ones. Raise `ValueError` when the rank of `F` is below its number of columns.
byKey.test-10: The third factor is the second given as a decimal, so the columns are dependent up to rounding. A test for a determinant of exactly 0 misses this; `np.linalg.matrix_rank` does not.
byKey.test-11: Three factors on two stocks cannot be independent. Raise `ValueError`.
byKey.test-12: With the ones column alone, the neutral signal is the score minus the average score, $0.1$.
byKey.test-13: These two factors are highly correlated but independent, so they must not be refused. The neutral signal is $(1, -1, -1, 1)$.
byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Check that `F` and `s` become float arrays and that you return a tuple of three.

explain.text: With independent columns, $\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{F}^T\mathbf{F})^{-1}\mathbf{F}^T$, which equals $\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{Q}^T$ from the reduced QR factorisation. The neutral part $(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{P})\mathbf{s}$ is perpendicular to every column of $\mathbf{F}$, so it carries no factor exposure. A rank of `F` below its column count, found by `np.linalg.matrix_rank`, flags dependent factors even after rounding.
